name: Zane Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Zane. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, no ties to companies, unions, parties or government, and this is all confidential. Could you tell me what a normal day at work looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I push dirt. I'm on a dozer at the Barlow open cut, the coal mine east of town, and mostly I'm cleaning up the benches and pushing the spoil, the waste rock, over the edge after the trucks dump it. Twelve-hour shifts, four on, four off. I like that nobody talks to me for most of it. I don't like the new screen they put in the cab, it beeps at me when I'm off the plan by half a metre.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been on the dozer?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three years. Before that I was thirty years at the sawmill in Harlan, on the log yard, until the mill shut when the big company bought it and moved everything south. I was fifty-five. Marlene does the books part-time at the hardware store, and between us we pay the bills and not much else. We've got maybe two or three weeks in the bank, no more. I'm still the guy the supervisor sends to the easy jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Fine by me. I've got enough trouble with the screen in the cab that beeps at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the crib hut I'd say let's see, same as I always do. I'm not one for big opinions. Somebody would say told you so, and I'd let them have it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't change much for me, because my worry was never clever computers. There's a dozer on the north side that a guy runs by remote from an office in town, and nobody talks about it in front of us. I'm the newest and slowest on the dozers, and the coal contracts are shrinking anyway, so if they cut a crew, I'm the first name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up and push dirt as well as I can, and try to get better on the steep benches so they stop giving me the easy jobs. I'd hold off replacing the fridge, because it still works if you kick it. Marlene would keep her book work at the hardware store, and we'd pay the bills and not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but quiet about it. Like the last year at the mill, when you could hear it coming if you listened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Marlene say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marlene would say we've got the house and we've got each other. Then she'd ask the hardware store for more hours without telling me. She did the same the year the mill shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you say the coal contracts are shrinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Barlow lost the power station contract out west two years ago, and they've been running one crew fewer since. Nobody needs a computer to cut a crew when the coal isn't selling. That's just business.

say: **Let's see**, same as I always say.
Somebody would say **told you so**, and I'd let them have it.
think: My worry was never **clever computers**; a dozer on the north side is already run from town.
I'm **the newest** and slowest on the dozers.
The **coal contracts** are shrinking, so if they cut a crew I'm first.
do: Keeps turning up and tries to get better on **the steep benches**.
Holds off **replacing the fridge**, which still works if kicked.
Keeps paying **the bills** on two small wages, with nothing much left over.
feel: **Anxious but quiet** about it, like the last year at the mill.
S0.quote: Nobody needs a computer to cut a crew when the coal isn't selling.
fieldNote: Zane's fear in a plateau has nothing to do with AI: it's **shrinking coal sales** and being the newest operator.
He has watched one workplace close with him in it, and **the mill** is his yardstick.
He mentioned **the remote dozer** on the north side almost in passing.

steps.text: Keep turning up and get better on the steep benches
Hold off replacing the old fridge

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, checking, buying. That's Marlene's job at the hardware store, near enough. Me, I'm in a dozer, so the robots being slow suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see, same as always. If anybody asked, I'd say dozers are dozers and somebody's got to sit in them for a while yet. I wouldn't say anything about Marlene to the guys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the first hit comes home, not to the pit. My wife Marlene keeps the books and does the ordering at the hardware store, and a program can do that now, so I'd say her hours go within a year. And once a computer plans the mine, that remote dozer on the north side gets a few brothers, and the newest operator is the one they don't need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut takeaways and the cable TV straight away and sell the boat trailer, maybe 1,500. I'd ask the pay office what my pension would be if I had to take it early at sixty. And I'd ask our daughter, quietly, whether we could lean on her if it came to that, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing the same sums I did when the mill shut, and they'd come out worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning the remote dozer system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They'd pick a young guy who plays video games, and I'd be sitting in a classroom looking stupid at fifty-eight. I'd rather be the guy who's always on time and never breaks anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Marlene the night her hours were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, I'm no good at that. I'd make the tea, say we'll manage, then go and sit in the truck in the driveway, the way I did after the mill closed.

think: The first hit comes home: **Marlene's book work** is what a program does now.
I'd say **her hours go** within a year.
Once a computer plans the mine, **the remote dozer** gets company, and I'm the operator they don't need.
do: Cuts **takeaways and cable TV** at once and sells the boat trailer for about 1,500.
Asks the pay office what **an early pension** at sixty would pay.
Asks his daughter quietly whether they could **lean on her** if needed.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake doing the mill-closing sums again, and they come out **worse**.

fieldNote: Zane placed the card's first blow on **his wife's bookkeeping**, which he expects to shrink within a year.

steps.text: Cut takeaways and cable TV and sell the boat trailer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking work in 2028. That's Marlene's job. The books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the break table I'd say the robots aren't here till 2031, so we've got a bit yet. I'd say it like I wasn't bothered. Then I'd go and sit in the cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's worse than the card makes it sound. That remote dozer on the north side is run by a guy in a room in town, and a computer that can think can sit in that room instead of him, so mine doesn't need any fancy robot. And Marlene's book work at the hardware store goes in 2028 for sure. So we could lose both pays inside a year or two, with three weeks in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the pay office in the first month and ask what my pension looks like if I take it at sixty, even with the chunk they take off. I'd work every overtime shift they'd give me. We'd sell the boat trailer and the second car straight away, maybe 6,000 for both. And I'd ask our daughter if we could lean on her for a while if it came to that, which would kill me to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the mill all over again, only quicker. I'd be lying awake listening to Marlene breathing and doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Marlene do when the books go to the computer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's sixty, same as me near enough. She'd look for shop floor hours, stocking shelves, that's still hands for a while. But the hardware store's not big, and there's ten people in town who'd want the same hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the card makes it sound better than it is. Why do you think the company would move early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they already have. Nobody talks about the remote dozer in front of us, and that tells you they're working out the numbers. I've already watched one place shut with me in it, and I didn't think I'd get a second go at that.

say: The robots aren't here **till 2031**, so we've got a bit yet.
I'd say it like **I wasn't bothered**, then go and sit in the cab.
think: A thinking computer can sit in **the remote dozer room**, so my dozer won't wait for robots.
**Marlene's book work** goes in 2028 too, so we could lose both pays within a year or two.
do: Asks the pay office in month one about **an early pension** at sixty, and works every overtime shift.
Sells the boat trailer and second car for **about 6,000**.
Asks **their daughter** whether they could lean on her if it came to that.
feel: Like **the mill closing** all over again, only quicker.
S2.quote: I've already watched one place shut with me in it, and I didn't think I'd get a second go at that.
fieldNote: Zane read the card darkly, because **the remote dozer** means thinking AI can do his job without robots.
**Marlene's bookkeeping** goes first, so both incomes are at risk at once.
He won't retrain; his plan is **an early pension**, selling things and leaning on family.

steps.text: Ask the Barlow pay office about taking his pension early at sixty
Sell the boat trailer and the second car for about 6,000
Ask their daughter if they could lean on her for a while

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031. I'd be sixty-three. That's closer to the pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a long time in mining, half the managers will have changed by then. At the break table I'd say 'let's see', same as always. I'd mean it a bit more this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the remote dozer room goes to the computer in 2031, and so do Marlene's books. I'd be 63. If I can stretch it to sixty-three with a bit in the bank, I can probably stretch the rest with Marlene finding shop hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save forty or fifty every pay, which means takeaways and the cable TV go straight away. I'd keep turning up and try to be good enough that they keep me to the end. And I'd wait and see if they keep a few dozer drivers on for the jobs the machines can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like a long drive with the fuel light on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning the remote system in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Five years or two, I'm still the guy who swears at the screen. Some young fella will do the room until the computer takes it. I'd rather keep my seat in the cab as long as they'll let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's in the bank by 2031 if you save fifty a pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the car doesn’t die, it adds up. Five or six thousand saved is not much, but it’s more than I had when the mill shut, and that counts for something.

think: The remote dozer room and Marlene's books go to the computer **in 2031**, when I'd be 63.
If I stretch it to sixty-three with a bit in **the bank**, Marlene's shop hours might cover the rest.
do: Saves **forty or fifty** every pay by cutting takeaways and cable TV.
Keeps working **well enough** to be kept to the end.
**Waits to see** if a few dozer drivers are kept for jobs machines can't do.
feel: **Anxious**, like a long drive with **the fuel light** on.
S3.quote: Five or six thousand saved is not much, but it’s more than I had when the mill shut, and that counts for something.
fieldNote: With five years Zane can see **a path** to near his pension.
Saving **small fixed amounts** makes him feel he's doing something, but he still refuses the remote system.
The **mill closing** is his yardstick for everything.

steps.text: Save forty or fifty every pay until 2031
Cancel the takeaways and the cable TV straight away
Wait to see if Barlow keeps a few dozer drivers for the hard jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036? I'd be sixty-eight. I'd be gone by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a long way off and I'll be fishing by then. I wouldn't say much else. The guys would joke I'm getting out just in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years isn't my problem, it's my grandson's problem, and that bothers me more than I thought it would. Kyle's sixteen and wants to drive machines like his grandad. By the time he's any good, the machines will be driving themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, keep putting a little by and pay off the car. I'd tell Kyle not to go into machine driving. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not for me. For the boy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kyle to do instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's the trouble. Something with people, maybe, nursing or the ambulance. I'd tell my grandson Kyle the dozer was good to me for a few years, but it won't be there for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the remote dozer still worry you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, the way it does now. But they've had that thing on the north side for two years and it's still one machine. If the computers don't get clever till 2036, I'll be on my boat by then.

The guys would joke I'm getting out **just in time**.
think: Ten years isn't my problem, it's **my grandson's problem**, and that bothers me more than expected.
**Kyle** wants to drive machines like his grandad, and by the time he's good, they'll drive themselves.

Tells his grandson Kyle **not to go into** machine driving.

S4.quote: I'd tell my grandson Kyle the dozer was good to me for a few years, but it won't be there for him.
fieldNote: Zane expects to **retire well before** 2036, so this picture barely touches him.

steps.text: Keep driving the dozer at Barlow until his pension
Put a little by each pay and pay off the car
Tell his grandson Kyle not to go into machine driving

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Marlene's book work goes first and my dozer right after, and you'd have no time and no money and the pension isn't there yet. What would help is being able to take the pension early without losing a big chunk of it, for guys over fifty-five who get pushed out. That, and somebody to do the forms for you.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask why they hire old guys like me if they're only going to get rid of us. I came here because the mill shut. If the mine shuts too, there's nowhere left to come to. That's this town in one sentence.

headlineQuote: I came here because the mill shut. If the mine shuts too, there's nowhere left to come to.
portrait: Zane Schmidt, 58, drives **a dozer** at the Barlow coal mine, after thirty years on a sawmill log yard that closed.
He has **two or three weeks** of savings, a wife who keeps books part-time, and no taste for screens.
In a plateau he's **anxious**, as the newest operator at a mine whose coal sales are shrinking.
Steady change **alarms** him, because Marlene's bookkeeping goes first and AI planning lets the remote dozer spread.
Fast AGI alarms him too; with five years he saves small amounts, and ten years worries him for **his grandson**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Marlene's bookkeeping and his dozer job could both go within a year or two.
There'd be **no money saved** and no pension yet.
whatWouldHelp: Taking his pension **early without losing** a big part of it if he's pushed out after fifty-five.
